transcript.content: Hello, thank you for coming in. Can you tell me what’s been bothering you or what brings you here today?

Well, doc, thanks for seeing me. I appreciate you taking the time. You know, you’d think when a guy finally stops working after doing it his whole life, he’d just kick his feet up, right? Maybe sit in the recliner, watch a little TV, finally enjoy the quiet. But what brings me in is that... well, since I stopped working, I just can’t seem to slow down. Not even a little bit. 

From the minute I wake up, I am up and moving. I’ll start on fixing a loose hinge on the back door, and then I'm out in the yard messing with the sprinkler head, and then I'm in the garage sorting coffee cans of old screws. It’s just one little job to the next, all day long, non-stop. It’s honestly like my brain thinks I still have a whole crew waiting on me to tell 'em what to do, you know? Like I'm still on the clock and we've got a deadline to hit. My wife says I'm wearing a trench in the floorboards with all my running around, and she's always telling me to just sit and drink my coffee, but I just... I can't seem to turn it off and take a breather. I just keep going and going.
Have you noticed your mood being unusually high, irritable, or energized along with this increased activity or restlessness since you stopped working?

No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. I mean, my mood is fine. I'm not walking around feeling on top of the world or irritable or anything like that. I'm not snapping at my wife or the neighbors, you know? Like, just yesterday, the neighbor's dog got into my flowerbed, and normally that might tick a guy off, but I just shooed him away and went back to fixing the fence post. 

And as for feeling energized in a weird way... it's not like that. It's not this big rush of energy or feeling like I can take on the world. It's more just... a motor. Like a low hum, you know? I wake up, I feel normal, but my body just says, "Alright, time to move." I'm not bouncing off the walls with some kind of crazy high mood, I just can't sit in the darn chair. My wife asked me the other day if I was feeling okay, because I was up at 6 AM organizing the tool shed, and I told her, "I feel fine, Martha, I just need to get this done." So, no, my mood is just... regular old me. Just a regular old me who can't seem to stop moving.
Have you noticed that you’re sleeping less since you stopped working, like needing less sleep but still feeling rested or energized?

Well, no, not exactly. I mean, it's not like I'm running on empty and feeling great about it, you know? I sleep... well, I sleep about the same as I always have, really. Maybe a solid six or seven hours, depending on the night and if my back is acting up. Sometimes that old mattress gets to me, and Martha's been saying we need a new one, maybe one of those memory foam things, but I don't know, I like a firm bed. Anyway, I go to bed around ten, ten-thirty, usually after we watch the evening news. I try to stay up for the late sports, but honestly, my eyes start getting heavy. 

So, I sleep my regular amount, and when I wake up, I feel rested, sure, but it's not like I'm waking up at 3 AM wide awake and ready to run a marathon. It's just normal sleep. It's just that once I *am* awake, usually around six, that's when the motor starts running. But it's not because I'm sleeping less or feeling some kind of unnatural energy. It's just... I wake up, I'm rested, and then I just have to start doing things. So, no, the sleep hasn't changed. I'm definitely not one of those folks who can get by on three hours and feel fine. If I get less than six, I'm dragging, even if I am still moving around all day. I'll just be moving around and yawning while I fix the sink.
Have you noticed that you need less sleep than usual without feeling tired, even if you’re not actually sleeping less?

Well, no, not at all. Like I was saying, if I don't get my regular sleep, I really feel it. It's not like I can just skip a few hours and feel perfectly fine the next day. I need my rest. Now, I know some folks, like my brother-in-law, Dave—he used to work the night shift down at the plant, and he swore he only needed four hours of sleep. Said he felt like a million bucks. But me? No way. If I get less than my usual six or seven hours, I'm definitely feeling it. 

I might still be out in the garage or the yard, because like I said, I just can't seem to sit still, but I'll be tired while I'm doing it. I'll be moving slow, making mistakes, dropping my wrench... Martha can always tell. She'll say, "You didn't sleep well, did you?" because she sees me out there dragging my feet. So, no, it's definitely not a situation where I feel like I don't need sleep. I need it just as much as I ever did, maybe more now that I'm getting older. My body definitely tells me when it's tired, even if my brain keeps telling me to get up and fix something. I don't have any of that magical energy where you just don't need to sleep. I wish I did sometimes, with all the projects I keep finding for myself around the house, but no, I definitely get tired if I don't sleep enough.

Have you been more involved in activities than usual, especially ones that are goal-directed, like starting multiple projects, making big plans, or getting overly involved in tasks around the house or with other people?

Well, no, not like big plans or anything out of the ordinary, really. I mean, I'm always doing something around the house, but that's just because there's always something that needs doing, you know? It's not like I'm suddenly deciding to build an addition on the house or start a new business or run for mayor. It's just the usual stuff. 

Like, last week, I did clean out the gutters, but that's because it's fall and the leaves are coming down. If you don't stay on top of the gutters, you get water backing up under the shingles, and then you've got a real mess on your hands. My neighbor, Tom, he ignored his gutters for two years straight, and he ended up having to replace a whole section of his roof. Cost him a fortune. So, I make sure I get up there. And while I was up on the ladder, I noticed some of the trim around the garage window was looking a little rotted, so I figured I might as well scrape that down and put a fresh coat of paint on it. And then, well, since I had the paint out, I touched up the mailbox post, too. 

But it's not like I'm starting a million new projects or getting overly involved in things. I'm just keeping up with the maintenance. You know how it is with an older house—you fix one thing, and you see two other things that need attention. Martha says I'm always puttering, but if I don't putter, the place falls apart. I'm not writing up grand blueprints or anything. I just see a loose hinge, and I grab my screwdriver. I'm not taking on the world, just trying to keep my own little corner of it from falling into disrepair. So, no, I wouldn't say I'm doing more goal-directed things than usual, just the same old chores that always need doing.
Have you ever experienced this kind of restlessness or inability to slow down before, especially during other major life changes or stressful times?

Well, let me think about that. You mean like when other big things happened in the past? No, I can't really say that I have. I mean, life is full of stressful times and big changes, right? That's just how it goes. Like back in, oh, it must have been '98, when they downsized the supply warehouse where I was working and I had to switch over to driving a delivery truck for a few years before I finally got on at the hardware store. That was a huge change, let me tell you. I had to learn a whole new route, deal with the dispatchers, and interact with the public a lot more than I was used to. It was stressful, sure, worrying about paying the mortgage and keeping food on the table. 

But I didn't get all jittery and restless like I am now, no. Back then, I just put my head down and did what I had to do. I'd come home dead tired, eat whatever Martha put in front of me, watch a little television, and go to sleep. I wasn't pacing the floors or looking for hinges to oil at eight o'clock at night. Even when the kids moved out—my daughter Sarah, she moved all the way out to Seattle for her husband's job, which was very hard on Martha, just very hard—I didn't get this way either. I just kept to my routine. I've always believed routine is important, you know? You get up, you go to work, you come home, you mow the lawn on Saturdays. 

So, no, I don't think I've ever felt quite this... wound up... during other changes or stressful patches. It's just now that I'm not punching a clock every morning, it's like my body just doesn't know how to sit in the recliner and watch a ballgame without my hands needing to do something. But before all this? No, I never really had this problem of not being able to slow down. I could always sit still just fine when the day's work was done.
Do you find yourself fidgeting, pacing, or feeling physically agitated, even when you're not actively working on something?

Well, yes, I suppose I do. It’s funny you ask it that way, because it’s not just when I’m out in the garage or trying to fix something. It’s when I’m supposed to be doing nothing at all that it really hits me. Take church, for instance. Martha and I go to the First Presbyterian down on Elm Street—we’ve been going there since the kids were little, must be thirty-five years now. Pastor Dave, he’s a good man, gives a solid sermon, usually about twenty, twenty-five minutes long. Nothing too crazy. But lately, sitting through that quiet time, or when he’s giving a longer talk, I just... I can’t seem to just sit there. 

I feel like I’ve got this motor running inside me. I’ll be shifting my weight from one side of the pew to the other, crossing my legs, uncrossing them. Then I start tapping my foot. Not loud, mind you, I don’t want to be disrespectful, but just a little tap, tap, tap on the carpet. And my hands, they need to be doing something, so I’ll pick up the hymnal, flip through it, put it back down, straighten my tie, check my watch. Martha will give me that look—you know the look, the one that says "settle down"—and I know I should just stay put and listen. I really do try. But it’s like my body is saying, "Get up! Go stretch! Walk down the aisle!" I have to fight the urge to just stand up and stretch my legs right in the middle of the closing prayer. 

And it’s the same thing if we go to a town hall meeting or even just sitting in the waiting room at the dentist. I just can’t seem to park myself and be still. I feel this... this tightness in my legs, like they need to be moving, and if I don't move them, I get all agitated. It’s not that I’m upset or anything, it’s just this physical need to shift around or pace. Sometimes I’ll even excuse myself to go to the restroom just so I can walk down the hall for a minute. So, yes, even when I’m not actively working on a project, I’m definitely fidgeting and feeling like I can't just sit peacefully.
Even if you're not sleeping less, do you ever feel like you could get by on much less sleep than usual without feeling tired?

Well, no... no, I definitely need my sleep. I’m not one of those folks who can just run on fumes, no sir. If I don't get my solid seven or eight hours, I am just useless the next day. 

I remember back when I was driving the delivery truck, sometimes they’d have me on a route that started at 4:00 AM, which meant I had to be up by 2:30. And if I hadn’t gotten to bed early enough the night before—say, if there was a late ballgame on or if Martha and I had company over—I’d be dragging all day long. Just dragging. I'd be drinking black coffee out of this big green thermos I used to carry just to keep my eyes open on the highway. It was miserable. 

And it’s the exact same way now. Even though I’m retired and I've got all this... this fidgeting and restlessness going on during the day, when nighttime comes, I am genuinely tired. I like to be in bed by 10:30, right after the local news wraps up. Once the weather report is done—we watch Bob over on Channel 4, he's been doing the weather for twenty years, very reliable—anyway, right after Bob gives the forecast, I brush my teeth and I'm out. 

If I happen to wake up in the middle of the night, say, to use the restroom, and I can’t get back to sleep for an hour or so, oh, I feel it the next morning. My head gets all foggy, I'm sluggish, and I can’t even focus on the morning crossword puzzle. Martha will be the first to tell you, a tired me is a grumpy me. I just don't have the patience for anything if I haven't slept. So, no, I never get that feeling where I think I could just get by on three or four hours and be perfectly fine. My body just demands a proper night's rest, always has. Even if my hands are busy all day long, when it's time to sleep, I really do need to sleep.

Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?

Well, no, I wouldn't say that at all. Honestly, I think I look forward to my bed just as much now as I did when I was working forty-plus hours a week. You see, even though I'm not physically hauling things or driving the truck anymore, all this... this pacing around and not being able to sit still that I was telling you about? It wears a guy out! By the time evening rolls around, I am absolutely ready to shut my eyes. 

I definitely still crave my sleep. It's not like I'm sitting there at night thinking, oh, I could just stay up until two in the morning because I don't have an alarm set. I know some fellas do that. My buddy Tom, he retired from the hardware store about a year before I did, and he tells me he stays up half the night watching old John Wayne movies just because he can. But not me. No, sir. If I try to push past my usual bedtime—say, if there's a really good college football game on that goes into overtime—my eyes just start getting incredibly heavy. I'll be sitting there in my brown recliner, the one by the window, and my chin will just start dropping to my chest. Next thing I know, Martha is tapping me on the shoulder telling me to go to bed because I'm snoring through the fourth quarter. 

So, no, the urge to sleep hasn't gone away or lessened one bit since I stopped working. I still need it just as badly. We actually bought a new mattress about, oh, it must have been four years ago now. One of those memory foam ones? Took some getting used to, I'll admit, because it feels a bit strange at first, like you're sinking into quicksand, but once you get used to it, it's wonderful for the lower back. Anyway, my point is, when ten-thirty hits, I am more than ready to get into that bed. I don't ever feel like I could just go without it or skip a few hours. My body still demands it just the same as it did when I was thirty.

Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?

Well, like I was just saying a minute ago, Doc, no, not at all. I know you're wondering if maybe my body just doesn't feel the *pull* for it as much since I'm not punching a time clock down at the depot anymore, but I promise you, I crave my sleep just as much as I ever did. 

You'd think being retired means you just float around and don't care about a schedule, but I really do. My brother-in-law, Frank—he retired from the postal service a few years back—he says he doesn't even know what day it is half the time, tells me he just sleeps whenever his eyes get heavy, maybe takes three naps a day and stays up till all hours. But me? No, I couldn't do that. I don't have that feeling where I could just skip my night's rest or go longer without it. 

If anything, I think my body craves it just as much because of all that nervous energy I burn through during the day, just pacing and fidgeting like we talked about. Just the other weekend, my daughter Sarah dropped her two kids off. They're six and eight, absolutely full of beans. We spent the whole Saturday out in the backyard, setting up this little inflatable pool for them, getting the hose hooked up—which was a whole ordeal because the spigot was leaking and I had to go dig out my wrench set to tighten the packing nut. Anyway, by eight o'clock that night, after they went home, I was sitting on the couch just counting down the minutes until I could hit that memory foam mattress I told you about. I didn't feel like I could go one extra hour, let alone skip it. If I tried to stay up and push through, I'd just be an absolute zombie the next morning. So, no, the actual craving for a good, solid night's rest hasn't changed one bit since my working days, I can assure you of that.

Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?

Doc, I feel like a broken record here, or maybe I'm just not explaining myself right, but no. I really, truly don't. I know you keep asking if I feel less of a need for it now that I'm not working, but I promise you, I don't have any sort of magic energy reserve that lets me skip out on my rest. 

Just this past Tuesday night, for example. Martha wanted to stay up and watch this new mystery show she found on one of those streaming things—our son installed a Roku stick on the back of the TV for us a few months back. Took him about five minutes to hook up, but I swear I still can't figure out which of the three remotes to use half the time. Anyway, she wanted to watch just one more episode because the last one ended on a big cliffhanger, you know how they do that to keep you hooked. It was only about 11:15, and I tried to stay up with her, I really did. I even went to the kitchen and poured myself a small glass of ice water to try and shock my system into staying alert. 

But my eyes? They felt like they had lead weights attached to them. I was nodding off right there on the sofa, completely missing all the clues. I ended up having to tell her she'd just have to fill me in on who the killer was in the morning because my body was absolutely screaming for the bed. I didn't feel like I could just push through it or go without it, not even for another forty-five minutes to finish a TV show. 

So, honestly, I don't know how else to say it—when my usual bedtime rolls around, I am done for the day. I crave that sleep just as much as I did thirty years ago, and I absolutely cannot go longer without it.

Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?

Doc, are... are you pulling my leg here? Because I swear we just went over this three or four times already. I don't mean to be disrespectful, I know you're the doctor and you've got your checklist on that computer or whatever you're looking at, but I really don't know how many other ways I can slice this pie for you. No. The answer is still no. I don't feel less of a need for sleep. I don't have some secret battery pack that suddenly kicked in just because I stopped working. 

I mean, if I didn't crave my sleep, I wouldn't have spent all that time telling you about how heavy my eyes get watching TV with Martha, or how much I love that memory foam mattress we bought. It's like... well, it's like my old Ford truck. When the gas tank is on empty, it's on empty. You can't just pat the dashboard and tell the truck, "Hey, you're retired now, you don't need gas to run." My body is exactly the same way. 

When it gets dark out, and the streetlights come on—we've got those new LED streetlights on our block now, by the way. The city put them in last fall and they are bright as all get-out, almost too bright if you ask me, you really have to pull the blinds shut tight or it looks like a UFO is landing in the front yard. But anyway, when it gets dark, my brain just says we're done. I need my rest, plain and simple. If I tried to go longer without it, I'd be completely useless the next day. I'd be grumpy, I wouldn't be able to focus on my crossword puzzles, and Martha would probably kick me out of the house. So, no, I definitely still crave my sleep just as much as I ever did. Are you sure you didn't mean to ask me a different question this time?

Doc... is this a joke? Am I on Candid Camera or something? Because I swear, my hearing is perfectly fine, and I know your hearing is fine, but we are stuck in a loop here. I don't know if your computer system is glitching and just spitting out the exact same sentence over and over, but my answer hasn't changed since the last three times you asked it. No. Absolutely not. I do not feel less of a need for sleep. 

I mean, look, back when I worked at the depot, I had this old wind-up alarm clock. One of those heavy metal ones with the two big bells on top, you know the kind? The thing sounded like a four-alarm fire when it went off. Martha absolutely despised it. She made me put it all the way across the room on top of the cherrywood dresser we got from her mother, just so I'd have to physically throw the covers off and walk over to shut it up. Because if it was next to the bed? I'd just smash the button and go right back to sleep, because my body needed the rest that badly. 

And what I'm trying to tell you is, if I still had that exact same clock today, I'd still have to put it on that dresser. Retiring didn't change my biology. I don't have this... this sudden ability to just run on fumes. If I get less than my usual amount, I am completely useless. I'll be nodding off in my armchair by two in the afternoon, dropping my crossword puzzle on the floor. 

So, for the record, one more time, with feeling: I need my sleep, I crave my sleep just as much as I ever did, and I cannot go longer without it. Now, please, tell me you have a different question on that screen of yours?

Doc, I... I really just don't know what to say anymore. Are you feeling alright? Did you hit your head this morning? Because I am sitting here, and you are sitting there, and you are asking me the exact same question for the fourth time in a row. I'm starting to think maybe you're the one who isn't getting enough sleep! 

I mean, look, I'll say it again, in plain English—no. I do not feel less of a need for sleep. I cannot go longer without it. It doesn't matter that I'm not working. 

Let me give you another example, since the alarm clock and the mystery show didn't do the trick. Just a couple of months ago, my daughter came over with the grandkids. It was a Saturday, and the boys wanted to stay up late and play that racing video game on the TV. Mario something. Now, I used to play the old games with my son back in the nineties—you remember those gray boxes where you had to blow dust out of the bottom of the game cartridge to get it to work? So I figured, sure, I'm retired, I don't have to be up for work, I'll stay up and play a few rounds with the boys. 

It got to be about 10:30, maybe 10:45. I was sitting in my good recliner, the brown leather one Martha got me from Macy's when I retired. The kids are yelling, the TV is flashing all these bright colors, they're throwing virtual turtle shells at each other... and you know what happened? I fell dead asleep right in the middle of a race. The little plastic controller just slipped right out of my hands and clattered onto the hardwood. Scared the absolute daylights out of our dog, Buster, who started barking his head off. But I was just gone. Out cold. 

Because my body needs that sleep! It doesn't care that I don't have a timecard to punch on Monday morning. When I hit my limit, I am done. So please, I am begging you, write it down in big bold letters on your chart: I need my sleep, I crave it just as much, and I absolutely cannot go without it. Now, can we please, please move on to whatever the next question is?

Doc. Seriously. I am looking right at you, and you are looking right at me, and you just read that exact same sentence again. Is this a test? Are you testing my patience, or my memory, or is your computer frozen? Because I feel like a skipping record player. You know, we used to have this old Zenith console stereo in the living room back in the late seventies, a beautiful piece of furniture, real wood veneer, not that particle board junk they sell at the big box stores nowadays. And if a record got a scratch in it, the needle would just bounce back and play the same three seconds of a Kenny Rogers song over and over until you got up and nudged it. I feel like I need to reach over that desk and nudge your computer mouse.

For the fifth time, and I really hope this is the last time because my jaw is getting tired, no. I do not feel less of a need for sleep. I need every single hour I can get. 

I mean, just yesterday, I was out in the backyard. I decided to clean out the gutters before the spring rains really start coming down. I got the aluminum extension ladder out of the shed, the one with the sticky latch on the third rung, I really need to spray some WD-40 on that thing, and I spent maybe two hours up there scooping out wet leaves and those little helicopter seeds from the maple tree next door. By the time I came inside and washed my hands, it was barely three o'clock. I sat down at the kitchen table with a glass of iced tea, and Martha found me twenty minutes later, snoring so loud I was vibrating the glass on the table. 

So no, my body craves sleep just as much as it did when I was working. Retiring didn't turn me into Superman. I am exhausted when I am exhausted. Now, please, can we talk about something else?

Okay, now I am genuinely, honestly concerned about you, Doc. Are you having a stroke? Should I call a nurse in here? Because I am not a medical professional, I just have a high school diploma and thirty years at the depot, but I know for a fact that asking a person the exact same question six times in a row is not standard procedure. I mean, is your keyboard stuck? Did somebody spill coffee on the mainframe? 

Look, I will say it again. No. N-O. I do not feel less of a need for sleep. I don't crave it less. I can't go longer without it. 

Just last Tuesday—Tuesday is senior discount day at the multiplex over on Route 9, the one that used to be a drive-in back in the eighties before they paved it over. Martha wanted to see that new movie, the really long one about the historical stuff in Europe. Three hours and fifteen minutes, the sign said. Now, I bought myself a large popcorn, the one where you pump the butter on yourself—well, they call it butter, but we all know it's just yellow soybean oil, but it tastes good anyway. So I'm sitting there in the dark, eating my popcorn, the movie starts, there are bombs going off on the screen, the surround sound is shaking the floorboards... and the next thing I know, Martha is elbowing me in the ribs because the lights are on and the teenager with the broom is waiting to sweep up our row. I slept through the entire second half of the movie. Drooled right on the collar of my good flannel shirt. 

So if I had this magical ability to go without sleep just because I don't clock in for work anymore, I think I would have managed to stay awake for a movie I paid eight dollars to see! My body demands sleep, Doc. It always has, and it still does. Now, I am begging you, please look at a different page on your clipboard or press a different button on your computer, because if I have to answer this again, I think my head is actually going to explode.

Okay, that's it. I am actively looking around the room for the hidden cameras. Is Alan Funt going to walk through that door? Because I feel like I am on Candid Camera, or the Twilight Zone, or maybe I'm the one having a medical emergency and this is all some sort of fever dream. Seven times, Doc. I have been counting. You have asked me that exact, identical string of words seven times. 

No! No, no, no, no, no. I do not feel less of a need for sleep. I need my sleep just as much as I did when I was thirty, probably more! 

I mean, good grief, just this past Sunday, Martha made a pot roast. Beautiful chuck roast, carrots, the little red potatoes—not the big russets, the little waxy ones with the thin skin you don't even have to peel, she just cuts them in half and throws them in the slow cooker. We ate around one o'clock, right after we got back from service. I went into the den to watch the baseball game. Just a regular season game, nothing crazy, but I like to keep up with the standings. I sat down on the sofa, kicked my shoes off—I wear those orthopedic walking shoes now, the ones with the velcro straps because my lower back gets stiff if I bend over to tie laces for too long, you know how it is getting older. 

Anyway, the game starts. First inning, lead-off guy hits a double down the third-base line. I lean back against the cushions. The next thing I know, I wake up, the room is completely dark, and the post-game show is on. The sun had completely set! I slept through nine whole innings of baseball. Nine! I had a little puddle of drool on my chin and a crick in my neck that I am still feeling today. 

Does that sound like a man who doesn't need sleep? Does that sound like a guy who can just skip a nap or go longer without resting just because he doesn't have to go down to the depot in the morning? My body shuts down when it's tired. It just pulls the plug. 

I'm begging you, Doc. I am literally pleading with you. If you ask me this one more time, I'm going to have to walk out into the hallway and find a nurse who knows how to reboot you, because you are stuck in a loop. No, I do not need less sleep. Please, for the love of everything holy, look at the next line on your paper and ask me something else.

Even though you’re getting the same amount of sleep, have you noticed that you feel less of a need for sleep since you stopped working — like you don’t crave it as much or could go longer without it, even if you still get your usual amount?
